Therefore, so that we may not seem to have passed over anything, but rather follow their examples, it will often be necessary to look back at the map; and since the account showed that the heights of the mountains stood out, by an ascent to the ridge of a very lofty summit we laboriously left markers built of stones, and the extent of the places is fortified and divided, which remains separate through the watersheds, a division well known on each side; other places keep the course of the banks; so that even if an enemy had wished to attack us, we could break them by fighting from the nearest bank. For around the coastal region we determined straight limits of compacted stones; we shall show the course of the whole straight line of the limits, because all colonies which are placed by the sea are bounded by the seashore. The fields of the valleys we arranged by ordinary law, and we named them intercisive. But on the plain we laid out the limits straight by levelling.

For the most part there are a great many fields assigned, and although the measure of their limits is different, yet they are also distant from one another, one from another, by 100 feet, by 150 feet, by 240 feet, by 300 feet, by 360 feet, by 420 feet, by 480 feet, by 600 feet, by 700 feet, by 840 feet, by 960 feet, by 1020 feet, by 10200 feet, by 10340 feet, by 10600 feet, by 10700 feet, by 10800 feet, by 20000 feet, yet in the long sight-line by which we drive the limit with markers.

If there is a thick narrow boundary-stone and on the other side a long, thick, doubled one, these two greatest limits are named the *decumanus* and the *cardo*. They run together for very many thousands of feet, and unless they end at the Alps, they divide the fields on the right and left of the straight lines that hold together with one another.
You must make every measure of this cultivation with the middle longer or wider: what is longer in width is a *scamnum*, but what is longer in length is a *striga*.
There are estates of the well-deserving, and they have been assigned narrower in proportion to the estimated fertility.

Lean and dry places are enclosed by a wider boundary. There are *subseciva* places, which do not belong to ordinary law, but if it is agreed among the possessors, let them possess [them]; if it is not agreed, [the land] remains in the power [of the authority].
Other more complete places are to belong to public law; just as many, if it is agreed by the possessors, they possess.

There are, moreover, these public places which are recorded as public woods and pastures of the Augustales, which can in no way be alienated, and they hold the guardianship either of public temples or of baths, which they call *locus collivus*.
Excluded land is that which lies between the boundary line and the centuries; it is called excluded because it is enclosed beyond the boundary limits.
Rubric on disputes.

The subject-matters of disputes are two, boundary and place; in the second of these is contained whatever is disputed concerning the land. But since the disputes marked in these parts also have various conditions, as far as I have been able to grasp, they must be named individually.

The kinds of disputes are 11: On the position of boundary-stones. On the region. On the boundary. On the place. On the ownership of a house. On possession. On alluvion. On the right of territory. On *subseciva* fields. On public places. On places left over and excluded. On sacred and religious places. On the inflow of rainwater, and on roads.

A dispute is between two or more neighbours. Between two, whether the boundary is in a straight course by reckoning of the rest; among several it makes a three-way boundary, in some places also a four-way boundary, according to the nearest possessions: while they do not know this, they do not agree, and the possessors themselves raise various disputes among themselves. Some litigate about the place, others about the boundary line, others attend to the estates. But first the origin of the case must be eagerly sought. By nature disputes of this kind arise through inheritances of this belief, wherefore there is litigation by ordinary law. First, however, let the question about possession be settled in court, and then let the land-surveyor be ordered to go to the places, so that, the truth having been made plain, a litigation of this kind may be ended.

The kinds of disputes arising from a river are these: not concerning fields that have been occupied, but what the force of the water has carried away will have no reclaiming; these are matters of the necessity of fortifying the bank, without another's loss, whoever it is who fortifies his own bank. But if the torrent of the river at some time runs down so violently that it changes its bed, it occupies the fields of many across the bank, and often also forms islands. But Cassius Longinus, a most learned authority on law and a judge, laid down this: that whatever the water carries away by lapping, the possessor must accept, since he ought, of course, to protect his own bank without another's loss. But if a greater force has rushed down, and changes its bed into another's boundaries, and an island is formed where it has run together, each must recognise the measure of the greater river, and he shall claim that island for himself whose land the storm seized, since it appears to have been snatched not by the possessor's negligence but by the violence of the storm.

*Subsecivum* land is registered according to its determinations; we enter it within its boundaries in the record-office of Caesar, and whatever has been granted as a benefaction or assigned to the colony, whether nearby or among other communities, we enter in the books of benefactions; and whatever else pertains to the surveyors' documents, not only for the soil of the colony, but also for the record-office of Caesar, must have [it] signed by the founder's hand.

Excluded and unassigned land is of a condition similar to *subsecivum*; if it has not been given to the commonwealth, to the Roman people, or to the colony itself by whose boundary it is surrounded, or does not belong to the Roman people, it remains in the power of him who was able to assign [it].
The markers of the boundary limits in various regions, whether names, villages, or possessions, these are the field evidences to be divided between both possessors.
In mountains, in dry and broken places, we find marked rocks.

On the summits of mountains [we find] *augustei* boundary-stones, that is, round ones, in the shape of a column, some marked with a letter; boundary chests; in places *grumi*, that is, heaps of stones; trees left standing, untouched by iron; a heap of rubble-walling, that is, where stones collected from both sides make the limit; likewise rocks, sacrificial altars, in places where untouched trees are seen to stand, at which place the ancients, wandering, used to make sacrifice. In another place military roads make the boundary, which are secured with a boundary-stone. Others, the right-hand sides of mountains, that is along the side of the mountain, the streams running by make the boundary. Sometimes tombs make the boundary; therefore tombs are to be followed, which, at the furthest boundaries running together, look to several junctions of fields. For all monuments testify to their owners.

There are *cursorii* boundary-stones set up in the shape of an inscribed stone, fixed places of a stream, boundary *cunabula* or *noverca*, which is built with rules, *scorpiones* where two wedge-shaped boundaries join. If perhaps in open country, where fields are laid out on the plain, they are found assigned in *iugera*. Likewise among the gullies of a crag, with untouched trees left standing, sacrificial ones as I said above, mounds of earth set up in the shape of a limit, millstones, pits or cones, ponds and *legonati*, and *calaviones* constructed by craftsmen. For sometimes [we find] squared and inscribed stones, which show whose field it is, who the owner is, how much space they guard. For not every marker stone is furnished with inscriptions, since in some places the stones are not inscribed, but are set in the shape of boundary-stones, which we call *cursorii*. For the mountains themselves too wholly determine places, but boundary-stones do not keep one measure between them, by the order of Augustus Caesar, through Balbus the surveyor, who distinguished and declared the measurements of all the provinces; and let the boundaries of places be fixed by the evidences written above.

There are, however, boundary-stones in which trust is not to be placed; these are called *itinerarii*. For all limits that divide the private boundaries on right and left, with a public road in the middle, must serve the public road: these are not such in all places; certainly a sign ought to be found under all boundary-stones; therefore what is found should be observed in place of a boundary-stone and should be kept, so that [the line] may be directed from one to one, and, if [there is] a mark, from mark to mark.

For such are the customs and observances of a fixed law: a sign has always been placed in all boundary-stones; we find either some ashes, or charcoal, or a potsherd, or bones, or glass, or a lump of iron, or bronze, or lime, or gypsum, or an earthenware vessel, which they also trampled down with certain fragments of stones and made fast with diligent care, so that it might stand more firmly. Such, then, was the sign they made between the owners between whom the boundaries were fixed. But boundary-stones are not in all places, but there are countless many other evidences; read [them] happily and take care to understand [them]; whoever understands what he sees can remove the strife and contest over fields. These surveyors, however, who are to judge, and those whom they call in as guarantors, must have prudence. In judging, moreover, the surveyor must act as a good and just man, so that he is moved by no ambition or sordid gain, and must preserve his reputation in measures and in conduct. For truth must be guarded by every craftsman; those are excluded who put forward false things as true. Some err through imprudence, some through lack of skill. Changing, therefore, in the profession the things generally added as true, through a dispute the craftsmen are compelled to measure argumentatively and conjecturally, even superfluously; but it will be necessary for the man who judges to be a safe craftsman in this.

You who wish to be a perfect geometer, read all these things that are set out in chapters below. For first of all one must know the art of arithmetic, which contains the causes and divisions of numbers, that is: what is the definition and division concerning even and odd numbers; — what is a composite number, and what an incomposite; — what is a perfect number, and what an imperfect; — what is a divisible number, and what an indivisible; — what is a superparticular number, and what a superpartient; — what is a superabundant number, and what a deficient; — what is a multiple number, and what a submultiple; — what is a solid number, and what a spherical; — how geometry was discovered; — what geometry is; — what its utility is; — what the order of the prescription is; — what is the method of the proposition; — of the disposition; — of the distribution; — of the description; — of the demonstration; — of the conclusion; — what a straight line is; — what the surface of a line is; — what a dividing line is; — how many kinds of extremities there are; — how many kinds of surfaces; — how many kinds of angles; — what a plane angle is; — what an obtuse angle is; — what a blunt angle is; — what a right angle is; — what an acute angle is; — what a divided measure is; — how much a stadium extends; — what an *acus* is; — what *climata* are; — what a *centua* is; — what a league is; — what an *arepennis* is; — what a *iugerum* is; — what a century is; — what a point is; — what a diameter is; — what a parallelogram is; — what a figure is; — what a circle is; — into how many parts the division is.
If you know all these things fully, you know the separation of places. For those who do not know the rule of this art put forward many false things as true.
Pupil. How was geometry discovered?
Master. The Egyptians say that geometry was discovered because of the need [to restore] the boundaries of the land, which the Nile flooded at the time of the inundation.
Pupil. Whence is geometry named?
Master. Geometry is named from the measuring of the earth, by which the boundaries of each piece of land are usually declared.
Pupil. What is geometry?
Master. Geometry is the discipline of magnitude and of the figures that are contemplated according to magnitude.
Pupil. What is the intention?

Master. Euclid's intention is twofold, looking to the pupil and to the natures of things. Looking to the pupil, because he must begin with these introductory matters for ease, for brevity, and so that for this reason there may be no difficulty in the questions. For the nature of things, because many things of physical science, and of the doctrine of Timaeus or Plato, are known to be demonstrated geometrically.
Pupil. What is the utility?

Master. The utility of geometry (as we said before above) is threefold: for livelihood, for health, for the soul: for livelihood, as for mechanics; for [health], as for physicians; for the soul, as for philosophers.
Pupil. What is the order of geometry among the disciplines?
Master. In one respect it is second after arithmetic, in another third.
Pupil. How is the inscription of the title to be understood?
Master. The prescription of the title is of the elements, which are the simpler figures, and from these others are composed which are also resolved into them.
Pupil. Is the book [Euclid's] own?
Master. This book is said to be Euclid's as to its arrangement; as to its demonstration or discovery it is said mostly to be of others.
Pupil. Into how many parts is it divided?
Master. This book is divided into four parts: on plane figures, on arithmetical matters, on rational and irrational lines, and on solids.
Pupil. What [parts] are there in a geometrical demonstration?
Master. Proposition, disposition, distribution, description, demonstration and conclusion.

It remains for us, however, to hand on a certain most profound discipline, which pertains most of all in reason to the integrity of the nature of all things. For great indeed is the fruit in this science, if one is not ignorant that goodness, defined and falling under knowledge and always imitable and perceptible by the mind, is the first nature, and perpetual in the beauty of its own substance, while the infinite disgrace of wickedness, resting on no principles of its own but by nature always wandering, is shaped by the principle of all definition as if impressed with some sign of the best figure, and is held back from that tide of error. For the mind, like a kind of ruler strengthened by pure intelligence, restrains excessive desire and the immoderate unbridledness of anger. We, however, have collected with moderate brevity what was discussed at greater length about numbers by Nicomachus, or set out about measures by Varro. And what, being passed over too quickly, offered too narrow an access to understanding, we have opened up by modest addition, so that at times, for the clarity of the matter, we have also used our own formulas and diagrams; how many vigils and how much sweat this cost us the sober reader easily recognises. And we have, as it were, collected these forms of inequality by labouring with tempered goodness; the reader himself will judge what we have drawn from the wealth of Greek letters into the treasury of Roman speech. If anything has shone forth from the teachings of wisdom, let it be approved through us by the judgement of the wisest. You see, then, reader, how the result of so great a labour awaits your examination alone, and does not venture to come before public ears unless it rests on the assent of a learned opinion; which should seem no wonder, since a work that pursues the discoveries of wisdom depends not on the author's judgement but on another's. For wisdom is the true knowledge and full comprehension of the causes and divisions of numbers; whoever spurns this, that is, the path of wisdom, I declare to him that he will not philosophise rightly. This, moreover, is arithmetic; for it is prior to all, not only because God, the founder of this worldly mass, had it as the first exemplar of his reasoning and established all things according to it, whatever things, fashioned by reason, found through number the concord of an assigned order, but arithmetic is declared prior also for this reason, that whatever things are prior by nature, when they are removed, the posterior things are removed together with them. But if the posterior things perish, nothing in the state of the prior substance is changed, as animal is prior to man. For if you remove animal, at once the nature of man too is destroyed. If you remove man, animal will not perish; yet properly the very nature of numbers preceded all things. All things whatever that were constructed by the primeval nature of things appear formed by the reason of numbers. For this was the principal exemplar in the mind of the founder; from this was derived the multitude of the four elements, from this the changes of the seasons, from this the motion of the stars and the turning of the heaven. Properly, moreover, by the very nature of numbers all the courses of the stars and the whole system of astronomy have been established. For thus we gather risings and settings, thus we keep track of the slownesses and speeds of the wandering stars, thus we recognise the eclipses and the manifold variations of the moon; since, as has become clear, the use of arithmetic is prior, let us take the beginning of the discussion from here; the same seems to occur in geometry or in arithmetic. For if you remove numbers, whence can we comprehend a triangle or a square, or whatever is treated in geometry, all of which are named from numbers? This will be plain if we understand that all inequalities have grown from [the] first beginnings [of equality], so that equality itself, holding as it were the force of mother and root, has itself founded all the species and orders of inequality. Let us take three twos, or three threes, or three fours, or as many beyond as one likes to set down. For what happens in these three terms happens likewise in the others. From these, then, according to the order of our rule, you will see first multiples born, and among these doubles first, then triples, then quadruples, and those following in the same order. Again, if the multiples are inverted, superparticulars will arise from them: from doubles the sesquialters, from triples the sesquitertians, from quadruples the sesquiquartans, and the rest in this way. From superparticulars inverted, superpartients must be born, so that from the sesquialter arises the superbipartient, the sesquitertian begets the supertripartient, and from the sesquiquartan the superquadripartient. When the former superparticulars are set upright and not inverted, multiple superparticulars arise. When superpartients are set upright, they produce multiple superpartients. These are the three rules: that you make the first number equal to the first, the second equal to the first and the second, the third equal to the first, two seconds, and the third. When you have done this with equal terms, those born from them will be doubles. If you do the same with these doubles, triples are produced, and from these quadruples, and so you will unfold to infinity all the forms of multiple number. Those whose parts have extended beyond what is enough are called superabundant, such as 12 or 24. For these, compared with their parts, obtain a greater sum of parts than the whole body: for the half of twelve is 6, the third part 4, the fourth 3, the sixth 2, the twelfth 1, and this whole heap overflows to 16 and surpasses the quantity of its whole body. Again, of the number 24 the half is 12, the third 8, the fourth 6, the sixth 4, the eighth 3, the twelfth 2, the twenty-fourth 1, which all return 36; in which it is clear that the sum of the parts is greater and overflows above its own body. And that [number is deficient] whose combined parts are surpassed by the quantity of the whole term, as 8 or 14; for eight has a half, that is 4, it has a quarter, which is 2, it has an eighth, 1, which all brought together collect seven, enclosing a sum smaller than the whole body. Again, fourteen has a half, that is 7, a seventh, that is 2, a fourteenth, that is 1, which, if collected together, grow to the sum of the number ten, smaller than the whole term. But those which are like the former, whose parts exceed it, seem like someone born with many hands beyond nature, or joined in a double body, or whatever monstrous thing nature has ever slipped in by multiplying parts.

But those [whose parts are] smaller [are like someone] who, as if some necessary part had been naturally taken away, was born lacking an eye, or cut short in some other limb, and so received a natural loss of the fullness of his whole. Between these, however, as between equal excesses, that number which is called perfect has obtained the moderation of the middle limit, an imitator of virtue, which is neither carried on by a superfluous advance nor, again, drawn back by a cramped diminution, but holds the mean; it neither runs riot with abundance in its equal parts nor lacks through poverty, as 6 or 28. For six has a half, that is 3, and a third, that is 2, and a sixth, that is 1, which, if they are brought into one sum, that is 3, 2, 1, the whole body of the number is found equal to its parts. And 28 has a half, 14, and a quarter, 7, and a seventh, 4, and a fourteenth, 2, [and] a twenty-eighth, 1, which, brought together, will equal the whole body with its parts; for the parts joined in one make 28. There is also in these a great likeness of virtue and vice: for you will find perfect numbers rarely, and they are easily counted, since they are few and produced in a very constant order. But superabundant ones you will find without limit, arranged in no orders, here and there and without order, and generated from no fixed end. The perfect numbers are, within ten, 6; within a hundred, 28; within a thousand, 416; within ten thousand, 800 and 128. And these numbers always end in two even [digits], 6 and 8, and the ends of the sums always come out alternately in these numbers. For first [comes] 6, then 28, after these 416, [ending in] the same six as the first; after that 800 and 128, [ending in] the same eight as the second.

There are five parts of number of greater inequality: one is called multiple, another superparticular, the third superpartient, the fourth multiple superparticular, the fifth multiple superpartient. To these five parts of the greater are opposed five other parts, which, one by one, are called by the same names in the species of the lesser, differing only by a prefix. For they are called submultiple, subsuperparticular, subsuperpartient, submultiple superparticular, submultiple superpartient. In the first part, if a number is multiplied, it is called multiple. In the second part it is called superparticular. In the third superpartient, then the fourth multiple superparticular. In the fifth multiple superpartient. But the lesser number, standing as one and the same in some part, is extended through the parts according to the rule and quantity of the greater.
Heading on even and odd numbers.

The table which is set below was made in this way: however many of the evenly even numbers in order the number three multiplied, whatever were produced from it were arranged in the first row. Again, those that were born when five was the multiplier were placed in the second place. Then those which seven produced by multiplying the rest we placed in the third place, and we do the same in the remaining part of the table. This, then, is the principle of the table set out above: if you look at the breadth, where there is one mean of two terms, and you join the terms themselves, you will find them double their own mean: 36 and 20 make 56, whose half is 28; and if you join 12 [and ...], they make 150, of which their middle term is found to be the half. But where they have two means, both extremes joined become equal to both means, as when you have joined 12 and 36 they make 48; if you add their means to each other, that is 20 and 28, they will make [the same]. And in the other part of the breadth the numbers which arise are noted in the same order, and in no respect did the principle of the two breadths differ. And you will observe the same in the same order in the other numbers, and this happens according to the form of the evenly odd number, in which, as was said above, this property lies. Again, if you look at the length, where two terms have one mean, what comes from multiplying the extremes, the same comes if the middle term takes the increase of its own quantity. For twelve times 48 make 576; and their middle term, that is 24, if it is multiplied [by itself], will produce the same 576 again. And again, if 24 is multiplied into 96, they make 2304, whose middle term, that is 48, if led into itself, the same 2304 are produced. But where two terms enclose two means, what comes from multiplying the extremes, this same is returned when the means are led into each other's sum. For twelve times 546 multiplied produce 'i5?, and their two means, that is 24 and 48, if multiplied into each other, will restore the same j 52; and this [is] in imitation of and in kinship with the evenly even number, from which, drawn by participation, this property is known to be engendered in it. And on the other side of the length the same principle and table is noted, from which it is clear that the whole number is produced from the two above, since it retains their properties. And since, naturally and according to the proper sequence of order, we placed the multiple species of inequality before all, and showed it to be the first species, although this will become clear to us in the order of a later work, here too, touching on it briefly, let us teach what we proposed most plainly and briefly. Let there be a table in which the natural order of continuous numbers up to ten is set in order, and in the second row the double order is woven, in the third the triple, in the fourth the quadruple, and so on up to the tenfold. For so we shall learn how the species of the multiple will be chief over the superparticular and the superpartient and all the others, and we shall at the same time look at certain other things, both most fine in subtlety, most useful for knowledge, and very delightful for exercise.

If, then, the first two sides of the table set out, which make an angle from one to ten and run on [to] ten, are looked at, and the rows beneath them are compared with them, which, beginning their angle from 4, set their end at twenty, the double, that is the first species of multiplicity, is shown, so that the first exceeds the first by unity alone, that is two [exceeds] one, the second passes the second by two, as four [does] two, the third the third by three, as six [does] three, the fourth surpasses the fourth by the amount of four, as eight [does] four, and in the same sequence all pass one another by the quantity of the lesser.

But if the third angle is examined, which, beginning from nine, extends the length and breadth on either side to thirty, and this is compared with the first breadth and length, the triple species of multiplicity appears, provided this comparison is made by the tenth letter, and these numbers will exceed one another according to the connection naturally made by parallelism: for the first exceeds the first by two, as three [does] one, the second the second by four, as six [does] two, the third the third by six, as nine [does] three, and the rest grow in the same manner of progression. This, indeed, natural wholeness itself put before us, with us contriving nothing outside, as appears in the very pattern of the table.

But if anyone wishes to compare with the ones above the term of the fourth angle, which is marked by the quantity of the number sixteen, and the length which ends at forty, setting the proportion side by side by the form of the letter *tO*, he will observe the quadruple quantity; and the progression over them is orderly, so that the first exceeds the first by three, as four [does] unity, the second beats the second by six, as eight [does] two, the third passes the third by nine, as twelve [does] three, and the following ones always pass over one another by an added amount of three. And if anyone looks at the angles beneath, the same will come about through all species of multiplicity up to the tenfold in a most well-arranged order.

But if anyone seeks superparticulars in this table, he will find them in this way. If he marks the second angle, whose beginning is four, and over which lies two, and fits the following row to it, the sesquialter proportion is shown. For the third [row] is sesquialter of the second, as three to two, or six to 4, or nine to six, or 12 to 8; and likewise, if such a pairing is made in the other numbers in the same series, no unlikeness of variation will slip in; yet the same exceeding of the sums is here too as was in the doubles. For the first exceeds the first, that is three [exceeds] two, by one, the second the second by two, the third the third by three, and so on. But if the fourth row is compared with the third, as 4 to 3, and you follow the rest in the same order, a sesquitertian comparison is gathered, as 4 to 3, or 8 to 6, or 12 to 9: do you see how in all these the sesquitertian is kept? Moreover, if, doing the same, you compare those beneath them with the following rows of the other, you will recognise all the superparticular species without any hindrance. And this is divine in this arrangement, that all the angular numbers are square. A square, to put it most briefly (it will also be explained more broadly), is called that which two equal numbers multiply, as is the case in this table too: for one once is one, and it is a square in potency. Likewise twice two are 4, three times three 9, which multiplications into themselves have made from their first elements. But those which are around them, that is around the angulars, are oblong numbers; and I call oblong those which numbers exceeding each other by one multiply: for around 4 are two and six, but two arises from one and two, when you have multiplied one by two. But unity is exceeded by two by a unit; and 6 [arises] from two and three, for twice three give six. And six and twelve enclose nine, and twelve arises from three and 4: for three times 4 make 12, and six from two and three, for twice three make 6; and all these are produced from sides greater by one. For since 6 arises from two and three, 3 exceeds the number two by one, and all others are of the same kind, so that they are produced from terms of the first and second row multiplied with each other, in such a way that what arises from the two oblongs placed on either side and twice the middle square is a square. And again, what arises from the two squares on either side and one middle oblong taken twice is itself also a square; and so that, of the angles of the whole table placed at the angular squares, of one angle the first is unity, of the other which is opposite, the third; while the angles on either side have the second unities; and the two angles of the angular squares make what is contained under them equal to that which comes from one of those angles which are on either side. For there are many other things which can be weighed in this table as useful and admirable, which for the present, for the sake of the restrained brevity of an introduction, we allow to remain unknown; but now let us turn our purpose to what follows.

The end of the book on Geometry of Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius. In this work, if anything more seems to anyone to be wanting, let him take it in good part; for we have corrected very many places, while in some it seemed best to leave each reader his own judgement and to change nothing rashly. Certainly, as far as could be done by diligence, industry and expense, nothing has been omitted by us.
